(d) Discuss with your counselor food allergies, food intolerance, and food-related illnesses and diseases. Explain why someone who handles or prepares food needs to be aware of these concerns. (e) Discuss with your counselor why reading food labels is important. Explain how to identify common allergens such as peanuts, tree nuts, milk, eggs, wheat, soy, and shellfish.

pamphlet_excerpts: Prioritizing Kitchen Safety: Safety is always a Scout's primary consideration (p. 64).
Emergency Injury Readiness: All good cooks should be prepared to take action should an injury occur (p. 64).
Cross-Contamination Prevention: They must know how to properly prepare and store foods to help prevent cross-contamination and avoid the spread of food-related illnesses (p. 64).
Recognizing Allergic Reactions: They should also be able to identify when individuals become sick because of an illness or allergic reaction (p. 64).
step_by_step_procedure: Step 1 - Separate Raw and Cooked: They must know how to properly prepare and store foods to help prevent cross-contamination and avoid the spread of food-related illnesses (p. 64).
Step 2 - Watch for Illness Symptoms: They should also be able to identify when individuals become sick because of an illness or allergic reaction (p. 64).
Step 3 - Follow Kitchen Safety Rules: Following the safety guidelines presented here will not eliminate your risk of a cooking injury but will help prepare you in case (p. 64).
Step 4 - Apply Basic First Aid: Basic first-aid techniques should be used when someone is injured while cooking (p. 64).

The requirement calls for Scouts to plan, prepare, and serve one breakfast, one lunch, and one dinner to at least one adult; those served need not be the same for all meals. requirements.req_text: Camp Cooking. Do the following: (a) Using the MyPlate food guide or the current USDA nutrition model, plan a menu that includes four meals, one snack, and one dessert for your patrol (or a similar size group of up to eight youth, including you) on a camping trip. These four meals must include two breakfasts, one lunch, and one dinner. Additionally, you must plan one snack and one dessert. Your menus should include enough food for each person, keeping in mind any special needs (such as food allergies) and how you keep your foods safe and free from cross-contamination. List the equipment and utensils needed to prepare and serve these meals. (b) Find or create recipes for the four meals, the snack, and the dessert you have planned. Adjust menu items in the recipes for the number to be served. Create a shopping list and budget to determine the per-person cost. (c) Share and discuss your menu plans and shopping list with your counselor. (d) In the outdoors, using your menu plans and recipes for this requirement, cook two of the four meals you planned using either a camp stove OR backpacking stove. Use a skillet OR a Dutch oven over campfire coals for the third meal, and cook the fourth meal in a foil pack OR on a skewer. Serve all of these meals to your patrol or a group of youth. (e) In the outdoors, using your menu plans and recipes for this requirement, prepare one snack and one dessert. Serve both of these to your patrol or a group of youth. (f) After each meal, have those you served evaluate the meal on presentation and taste, and then evaluate your own meal. Discuss what you learned with your counselor, including any adjustments that could have improved or enhanced your meals. Tell how planning and preparation help ensure successful outdoor cooking. (g) Lead the clean-up of equipment, utensils, and the cooking site thoroughly after each meal. Properly store or dispose of unused ingredients, leftover food, dishwater and garbage. pamphlet_excerpts: Evolving Food Industry Careers: Careers in the Food Industry With greater innovation and new emerging technologies, more career paths within the food industry evolve every year (p. 79).

patrol_quiz_bank.scenario_prompt: While preparing chicken fajitas at camp, a Scout uses a plastic cutting board and chef's knife to slice raw chicken breast, and then reaches for fresh bell peppers and tortillas to slice for a cold side salad. What food-safety step is required first?
patrol_quiz_bank.question: While preparing chicken fajitas at camp, a Scout uses a plastic cutting board and chef's knife to slice raw chicken breast, and then reaches for fresh bell peppers and tortillas to slice for a cold side salad. What food-safety step is required first?
options: A. Wipe the knife blade on a dry camp towel and slice the raw vegetables on the same board.

B. Prevent cross-contamination by using a separate cutting board for produce, or washing, rinsing, and sanitizing the board, knife, and hands thoroughly with hot soapy water and sanitizer solution before touching ready-to-eat food.
C. Leave the raw chicken sitting in the sun at 75°F for 4 hours before cooking.
D. Rinse the cutting board briefly in cold creek water without soap or sanitizer.
choices: A. Wipe the knife blade on a dry camp towel and slice the raw vegetables on the same board.

B. Prevent cross-contamination by using a separate cutting board for produce, or washing, rinsing, and sanitizing the board, knife, and hands thoroughly with hot soapy water and sanitizer solution before touching ready-to-eat food.
C. Leave the raw chicken sitting in the sun at 75°F for 4 hours before cooking.
D. Rinse the cutting board briefly in cold creek water without soap or sanitizer.
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: B. Prevent cross-contamination by using a separate cutting board for produce, or washing, rinsing, and sanitizing the board, knife, and hands thoroughly with hot soapy water and sanitizer solution before touching ready-to-eat food.
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Raw poultry carries Salmonella and Campylobacter; transferring raw juices to ready-to-eat produce causes acute food borne illness unless surfaces are sanitized and perishables stay out of the 40°F-140°F danger zone.

C. Its thick cast-iron walls distribute and hold heat evenly around the food
D. It requires no preheating or seasoning before cooking acidic stews
choices: A. Its thin aluminum walls cool down immediately when removed from coals

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (C): A Dutch oven has thick walls that retain and distribute heat evenly, making it ideal for baking, roasting, and slow simmering at camp (p. 24).

patrol_quiz_bank.question: How should a patrol handle food scraps and wash water when cleaning up a camp kitchen under Leave No Trace principles?
options: A. Wash pots directly in a creek so flowing water carries bits downstream
B. Bury leftover food scraps six inches deep next to the tent site
C. Burn all aluminum foil and wet food waste in the campfire ring
D. Strain food particles into sealed trash bags to pack out and scatter wastewater away from water sources
choices: A. Wash pots directly in a creek so flowing water carries bits downstream
B. Bury leftover food scraps six inches deep next to the tent site
C. Burn all aluminum foil and wet food waste in the campfire ring
D. Strain food particles into sealed trash bags to pack out and scatter wastewater away from water sources
patrol_quiz_bank.correct_answer: D. Strain food particles into sealed trash bags to pack out and scatter wastewater away from water sources
patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (D): Following Leave No Trace and the Outdoor Code requires straining food particles out of dishwater, packing out all solid waste, and disposing of wash water properly away from natural water sources (p. 50).

B. To reduce bulk, weight, and leftover trash that must be packed out
C. To increase the calorie density of dehydrated grains
D. To avoid having to measure water at the campsite
choices: A. To keep food frozen without carrying dry ice

patrol_quiz_bank.explanation: Correct Answer (B): Repackaging trail food removes heavy cardboard boxes and cans, pre-measures portions by meal, and minimizes trash that must be carried out on the trail (p. 21).
